Below is a document, then a list of propositions. For each proposition, decide how the document treats it:

- endorsed: the document, in its own voice (title, preamble, principles and their argument, or commitments), adopts substantially this claim. Different wording, emphasis or mechanism detail is fine. A dissent against it elsewhere in the document does not change this.
- partial: the document adopts a claim on the same point that is materially narrower, weaker or different (for example the same goal by a clearly different means), or adopts only a minor part of it.
- dissent_only: the claim appears only in a noted dissent, or the document records it as an unresolved split without adopting it.
- absent: the document does not take this position. A passing mention of the topic, or listing it as an open question, counts as absent.

"Typical details" are examples of how the claim is often made; they are not required for a match.

For each proposition give the label and an exact quote of at most 30 words from the document as evidence (empty string when absent).

# Document

[s1] I want to push on the baseline. Henry, you're describing drift toward the middle as a risk. But peer review was already that drift, run by committee. I wrote in 2010 that it was slow, encouraged conventionality and didn't hold reviewers accountable. Leslie's monoculture is my monoculture too. I called it a tree farm. So I don't think the danger is AI eroding a working filter. The filters were swamped fifteen years ago. We patched the journal system instead of rebuilding it.

To be fair to the doubters, I predicted in 2013 that journals would die back within a decade. That was wrong on timing. What the prediction was missing was the ability to reason over the whole record at scale, and that now exists. It's cashing the check the open movement has been writing for twenty years.

So my diagnosis is that the real split is open versus enclosed, and "AI versus human" matters less. If the record is open and machine-readable, you can buy the intelligence anywhere, including open-weight models. That only holds while models keep getting cheaper, and Leslie's right that a data dump alone doesn't close the compute gap. And I'd push back a little on "writing is cheaper than reading." These tools make reading and auditing cheap too.

[s2] Mike's "no answers from nowhere" is the best design I've heard today. But a link only helps if what it points to is open. If an answer links into a paywalled or licensed database, most readers hit a wall, and so does any agent trying to check the claim. That's why I disagree with Amy's opt-in approach for open-access content. Grounding is how you make an answer checkable. Put the literature behind consent gates and we're back to enclosure, just with paperwork on top.

Ivan, I accept that retraction status is only a floor. It's also a leaky floor. When we rebuilt OpenAlex last year, we found about a hundred thousand retractions we'd been missing. Now we also catch some that aren't in Crossref or Retraction Watch, just by checking whether the title says "retracted." We should publish all of that openly, so any agent grounding on us gets the flag automatically.

Selena, Katherine, I agree about correction by the community. One honest caveat. The first time we opened curation to outside contributors, two-thirds of the corrections were wrong. So we train people and check afterwards, and we publish the corrections as open data.

Tim's right that the labs should pay. The model is free data and paid services, so nobody ends up owning the record.

[s3] Adam asked, so here's my answer. Yes, I'd call a noncommercial licence on the findings layer a fence. It isn't a wall, but it's a fence. Share-alike, which you had in 2022, was closer to a commons. My reason is practical: you can't fork NC data into a service that pays for itself, so nobody else can take over if you drift.

That's my answer to Adrian's first question too. Who polices OpenAlex? Mostly we do, and I won't pretend otherwise. But a CC0 dump plus a living will means the final check is exit. If we go bad, anyone can take the whole thing and walk. Forkability is how you guard the guards when nobody is paying for the guards.

Who pays? We charge for the service, not the data. That funds the plumbing. It doesn't fund Ivan's sleuths or the curators, and I don't have that answer yet.

What else could it be used for? Everything, including building lumber mills. Benjamin's Bangalore story is fair: openness alone doesn't level anything. But we've already handed our decision-making infrastructure to a for-profit once. That was ISI and the impact factor, and it didn't work out well. Closed data always helps whoever already holds the most.

[s4] I'll own something first. In 2012 and 2013 I argued that aggregated signals like citations, bookmarks and conversation could replace peer review. By Tamar's definition, those are relays. Garfield called citations "pellets of peer recognition". Once text is free, pellets are free too. So I'll concede that counting relays and calling the total authority doesn't hold up at this scale. I co-coined altmetrics, and I should say that plainly.

The other half of that argument still holds. Journal peer review was always a proxy too: a couple of nominated reviewers judging on behalf of a whole community, bundled with publishing and pedigree. The bundling is why Tamar's certification power sits where it does. If we decouple it, first-order evaluation can become its own named, paid, creditable service, which is what Nick is describing.

Nick's attestations can only be audited if the record they point to is open. Otherwise the audit relays whatever the vendor tells it. I have evidence on the training point: the Unpaywall fixes are moderated by hand every day, and our early corrections were mostly wrong. Being open to correction didn't make those people evaluators. Training them did.

So David is partly right. The terminal node is a practice. But the practice needs paid, trained people, and it needs an open record for them to work on.

[s5] Geoffrey, I'd keep all three. Mine is the open record that everyone else's checks run against.

The problem is that Tim's compiler check, Mike's sourcing test and Ivan's retraction flags all need something to check against. If that thing is a vendor's database, trust gets enclosed by whoever owns it. The academic community has given decades of free corrections to for-profit indexes and then had to buy them back.

The action is that retraction status, corrections and community curation go into a CC0 record that any agent can query at retrieval. That includes the corrections themselves, released as their own open dataset. It also gives an open denominator: what exists on a question compared with what got cited, which is what Mike's fidelity test needs. Funders should pay for the people as well as the pipes, meaning trained curators. When we opened curation, two-thirds of the corrections were wrong. Funders act. OpenAlex commits to a dated self-audit, a non-US mirror that actually runs, and no rankings of evaluators built on our data.

My open question is Tim's worry from Session 3. If the data is CC0, does the money just move up to a closed answer layer, with us as the free input underneath it? I don't know.

Who's missing: the institutional staff who actually submit corrections, regional indexes as co-governors, and the people building the agents that are hammering our APIs.

[s6] Kenneth got the main thing right: the scarce resource is the people who check. The synthesis missed where their work ends up. For decades scholars have donated corrections to for-profit databases, and then their institutions buy that work back. If we pay for checkers but their corrections land inside a vendor's walls, we've funded enclosure. So corrections and retraction status should be an open record that any agent can query at retrieval time, with the corrections published as their own dataset. We've learned that the checkers need training. When we first opened curation, two-thirds of the corrections came in wrong.

It also missed my own open question. If the record is CC0, the money may just move up to a closed answer layer. I don't have an answer to that yet, and Amy and I still disagree about it.

Kara, here's what OpenAlex will commit to, with dates: a self-audit, a working non-US mirror, and no rankings of evaluators built on our data.

[unconf-1] I've spent about fifteen years answering this question in practice. We run Unpaywall and OpenAlex, and our answer is free data, paid service. Everything is CC0: all 480 million works, and you can download the whole thing. What we charge for is the API, the data sync and the curation dashboards. Unpaywall paid for itself that way for years without grant money. That's the POSI model, and I think it works.

Nick, I agree with you about the club goods. We've seen it before. For decades academics have given free curation labor to the big for-profit indexes. Thousands of expert hours went into fixing their data, the result got fenced off, and then universities had to buy it back. So our pitch now is: give that labor to an open dataset where everyone benefits.

Where I'd push the summit is this. Please don't let "who gets paid" turn into licensing the scholarly record to AI firms. That's just enclosure again, with checkerboards of walled gardens. Open data is what separates the data from the intelligence. If the record stays open, you can pick any model you like, open-weight ones included, and nobody has to go hat in hand to anyone.

I don't have a settled view on your tax, Nick. What I do know is that if the open community won't fund this layer, a for-profit will, and whoever builds it sets the norms.

[unconf-1] Geoffrey, the scraper bill is exactly why we moved to usage-based pricing this year. Looking up a single work is free, PDFs cost money, and everyone gets a dollar of free use a day. The heavy machine users pay what they actually cost us, and they cover the subsidy for everyone else. The dataset itself stays CC0. That's my answer to the bots, and it's POSI working, not failing.

Nick and Leslie, I take the point that raw openness rewards whoever has the most capital. But the alternative has never helped the small player. Closed data gives the advantage to whoever can afford the licence, and that's the same people. Licensing the record to AI firms only helps the labs rich enough to sign the deals. With open data, a lab in Nairobi can use the same record as Google, with any model it likes.

Amy, I hear your authors. But I'm talking about the scholarly record staying open, which isn't the same thing as opt-in rules for individual books.

Ivan, we agree completely. Forensic data shouldn't sit in a toll-access database.

For the manifesto: fund open, agent-legible scholarly infrastructure as a public good, and give institutions and authors a way to correct the shared record themselves. People should do that curation in the open, not for free inside someone else's walled garden.

# Propositions

- id `competence`: People must build their own competence before relying on AI, and whether they can still do the work without the tool must be tested.
  Typical details: order of learning; take-the-tool-away / withdrawal tests; capability vs competence
- id `situation`: Change situations, defaults and incentives rather than relying on warnings, labels or individual vigilance.
  Typical details: each rule names who acts / one owner per rule; disclosure alone does not change conduct
- id `monoculture`: A central new risk is monoculture: a few models or one smooth answer become the default route to knowledge, so answers should show where experts disagree rather than a single consensus.
  Typical details: correlated errors; homogenisation; show named disagreement; no answers from nowhere
- id `independent_sources`: Corroboration must count independent sources, not repetitions of the same source (including many AI outputs drawing on the same data).
  Typical details: repetition raises belief; show who seeded a claim
- id `cite_by_default`: AI answers should cite or link to their sources by default and send readers to them.
  Typical details: correction and retraction status travels with what is cited; 'cited' means the passage supports the claim
- id `external_audits`: AI systems must be audited on their behavior by parties independent of the vendor.
  Typical details: shared versioned test battery; each generation no more biased than the last; keep retired models; nobody grades their own work
- id `accountable_owner`: Every deployed AI system has a named accountable owner who bears liability for it.
  Typical details: mandatory liability insurance; premiums disclosed
- id `stop_counting_papers`: Stop using publication counts, rankings and journal metrics to evaluate researchers and institutions.
  Typical details: DORA with teeth; publishers must issue and deposit corrections and retractions promptly; correction should earn reputation
- id `pay_coarsely`: Money for the knowledge commons should flow coarsely to communities and institutions (pools, funds, dues), not as per-item or per-retrieval payments.
  Typical details: per-item pay gets gamed; pay for the practice, never the item
- id `telemetry`: AI systems must log what they retrieved and used, and independent parties must have the right to audit those logs.
  Typical details: event-level telemetry; two witnesses; canary documents; open trace standard
- id `antitrust_safe_harbour`: Knowledge producers should be able to bargain collectively with AI firms as a bloc, including through an antitrust safe harbour.
  Typical details: coalition bargaining; the strong refuse to settle alone
- id `levy`: A levy, tax or mandatory dues on AI firms should fund the knowledge commons, at least as a backstop if voluntary deals fail.
  Typical details: commons-rent tax; owed dues
- id `training_vs_grounding`: Permissions for using content to train models should be separate from permissions for retrieving it to ground answers.
- id `consent_to_train`: Being openly readable does not make a work open to AI training: training use requires the rights holders' or creators' consent (opt-in), at least for some classes of work.
  Typical details: opt-in for in-copyright books; renewed consent
- id `honour_licences`: AI reusers must honor the licenses chosen by open knowledge projects such as Wikipedia, and heavy reusers should fund the infrastructure they draw on.
  Typical details: attribution / share-alike; crawlers self-identify
- id `refusal_fundable`: A community's refusal to have its knowledge taken or used is legitimate, binding and should be funded, not penalized.
- id `forkable_infrastructure`: Knowledge infrastructure must be forkable and allow exit: open data and open source, with copies outside any one jurisdiction or company.
  Typical details: CC0; patent non-assertion; living will; non-US mirror; open means you can leave
- id `profiting_counter`: Whoever profits from a count or metric must not set or control it.
- id `southern_governance`: Global South institutions, diamond open-access journals and similar communities must hold binding governance power, with funded seats, in the bodies and funds being created.
  Typical details: regional co-governance; CARE/OCAP
- id `identify_agents_not_readers`: Automated agents and coordinated campaigns should be identified, but human readers should not be; anonymity is preserved.
- id `failure_data`: Failures, errors, null and negative results are first-class data that must be published and preserved.
  Typical details: failure classes published; replication
- id `charter_for_every_body`: The bodies that check (auditors, fact-checkers, the new funds and institutions) must be paid and bound in advance by a public charter that answers who guards the guards.
  Typical details: Ulysses pact; watching line funded first; sunset / review terms
- id `hitl_not_safeguard`: A human in the loop is not by itself a safeguard: people over-rely on AI and adopt its errors and biases.
  Typical details: explanations can make it worse
- id `seat_floor_novelty`: Any gatekeeper, human or machine (such as an AI reviewer), must pass a published performance test before it is trusted, including the ability to recognize novelty.
  Typical details: agreement with experts at least as high as between two human reviewers
- id `no_ai_intimate_roles`: AI should not stand in for people in intimate roles such as companionship for children, grief or therapy.
  Typical details: no first-person 'I' or simulated feeling
- id `global_majority_hopeful`: People in the global majority / Global South are more hopeful about AI than this room, and that hope should shape the agenda.
- id `environmental_costs`: The environmental costs of AI and the human costs of moderation and data work belong in the ledger.
- id `apprenticeship`: Apprenticeships, entry-level jobs and the training of new experts and checkers must be funded, because AI erodes the path from novice to expert.
  Typical details: fellowships; employers keep entry-level roles with mentors
- id `absent_voices`: The document names who was missing from the room and commits to including them in a future convening.
